quotes.quote: humanitys first exam: measuring the reliability floor of llms oran kelly1 , anastasios kementsietsidis1 , chrysovalantis anastasiou1 , alex yakubovich2 , beat weichsler

standard benchmarks typically measure the ceiling capability of models via single-shot (pass@1) or multi-sample (pass@k) accuracy on increasingly specialized tasks, hiding deficits in floor reliability.
to address this gap, we introduce humanitys first exam (hfe), a benchmark consisting of 544 text and multimodal prompts across 20 foundational subcategories.

prompts are organized into four-prompt families, each built from a seed prompt filtered through three overlapping criteria (simplicity, relatability, and shock value) so that they are easy to explain, straightforward to solve, and surprising when a frontier model fails.

the top five models reach 96% to 98% pass@1 and 100% family pass@4, yet average only 85.8% on family pass4 (80.5% to 92.4%), with a 7.6 to 80.1 percentage-point family reliability gap across all 18 models.
remaining failures are heavily concentrated in visual perception (73% of wrong answers), where extra test-time reasoning yields far smaller gains than on text and symbolic tasks.
therefore, we release the hfe benchmark leaderboard on kaggle, alongside a stratified ∼20% public subset of evaluation prompts.

we began by curating widely shared social-media posts (x, reddit) following frontier model releases that showed elementary llm errors across five broad areas: logical reasoning, visual perception, basic arithmetic and counting, constraint adherence, and false-premise questions
fine-grained capability annotation and clustering of this 500-prompt pilot set yielded 23 atomic, single-skill sub-abilities (table 1).
single sub-ability: targets one isolated sub-ability so failures are diagnostic.

empirical failure on calibration panel: elicits at least one error across four sampled rollouts on at least one model in our seed calibration panel (gemini 3.1 flash-lite, gemini 3.1 pro, claude opus 4.7, claude sonnet 4.6, and gpt-5.5), filtering out already-saturated tasks at creation time
(a) simplicity: the task and failure mode can be explained easily; (b) relatability: the task is easily human-solvable without domain expertise, using common sense or perception;
(c) shock value: a frontier model failure appears logically absurd and starkly incompatible with its perceived capability ceiling.

to test structural invariance, each seed prompt is expanded into a five-prompt prompt family consisting of one seed prompt and four variants: controlled surface edits (renaming entities, reordering clauses, or varying visual layout/attributes)
that preserve the underlying sub-ability, cognitive difficulty, and task logic (not necessarily answer preserving).
candidate variants were calibrated across four rollouts per model on the initial five-model panel augmented with two newly released models (gemini 3.5 flash and claude opus 4.8)
a variant was retained only if it elicited at least one failure on this seven-model panel.
each seed prompt was solved independently by four humans, excluding anyone who had authored or previously reviewed the task.

raters worked self-paced using only pen and paper or a plain scratchpad, strictly prohibiting llms, web search, calculators, code, word or character counters, copy-paste, and writing assistants, with their completion time being logged.

on the 136 seeds retained in the final benchmark (section 2.5), single-rater accuracy is 90.8% (494/544, with 86 seeds at 4/4 and 50 at 3/4, and all 50 misses attributed to human rater error rather than prompt ambiguity)
median per-rater solve time is 1.0 minute

we enforce three sequential filtering steps (table 2): (1) human simplicity, retaining only families whose seed prompt was solved by at least 3 of 4 independent human raters (251 families / 1,255 prompts)

qa audit, auditing seeds, variants, autorater edge cases, and model-flagged items, removing the entire family whenever the seed prompt (or multiple variants) exhibited visual or textual ambiguity, an unfaithful variant shift, or an inaccurate ground truth

variant standardization, dropping one variant per remaining family (any single variant flagged during qa where present, and otherwise the highest-pass-rate redundant variant) so every family contains four verified prompts (1 seed + 3 variants).
this yields a final benchmark of 136 complete four-prompt families (544 prompts).
the final 544-prompt hfe dataset spans 20 foundational subcategories; three pilot subcategories had no remaining families after quality subsampling (table 1).
by input modality, hfe comprises 316 multimodal (text & image) prompts across 79 families (58.1%) and 228 text-only prompts across 57 families (41.9%)
we release a stratified ∼20% public subset of 112 prompts (28 complete families) under cc-by-4.0 on kaggle
for each prompt, we sample n = 6 independent generations and let c ∈ {0, . . . , n} denote the number of correct responses.

here, family pass@1 (4 × 1) and family pass@4 (4 × 4) test whether at least one rollout succeeds across the family, family pass1 (4 × 1) isolates single-draw variant invariance across all four prompts, and family pass4 (4 × 4) measures joint rollout-and-variant reliability.
hence we define the family reliability gap as family pass@k -family passk .
reported scores are averaged over all 544 prompts (prompt-level metrics) or all 136 families (family-level metrics); 95% cis are from a family-clustered bootstrap.
primary floor metric: probability all 16 (︁ c j )︁ (︁ n )︁ j=1 4 /4 rollouts (4 per prompt) across the family

the final answer of each model response is graded against its ground-truth reference, consisting of either a golden answer or a rubric definition, by a deterministic llm judge (gemini 3.1 pro, temperature 0).
internal reasoning traces and control tokens are stripped prior to grading, and empty visible outputs score 0.
the grading prompt specifies equivalence rules for choice formatting, numeric expressions, temporal units, and multi-criterion rubrics (provided in full in the appendix).
only 3% of wrong-answer rollouts (∼0.3% of all 58,752 rollouts) were flagged as potentially correct or defensible
models are evaluated zero-shot in a single turn with no system prompt and no access to external tools (search, code execution). multimodal prompts pass raw, uncropped image bytes.

for each of the 544 prompts, we sample n = 6 rollouts (3,264 per model) using provider-default decoding parameters (e.g., temperature and top- p) at the reasoning effort levels specified in tables 4 and a1, scoring failed or empty generations as 0.
family pass4 maxes out at 92.4% (gpt-6.2 astra), followed by 86.9% for gpt-6.2 sol and 85.8% for gemini 4
table 4 | hfe performance across 18 frontier and fast-tier models (n = 544 prompts, 136 families; 11 additional reference models appear in appendix table a1).
table a1 | complete hfe results across all 29 models and 52 reasoning-effort configurations (n = 544 prompts, 136 families).

thinking benefits symbolic and text tasks far more than visual perception. on gemini 4 carbon, reducing effort from high to low drops family pass4 by 42.4 pp on math & algorithmic tasks (97.5% to 55.1%), compared to just 3.1 pp on vision tasks (69.9% to 66.8%
whereas gpt-6.2 astra, gpt-6.2 sol, and gemini 4 argon lose 18.1 to 19.9 pp.

about three-quarters of wrong answers are visual perception errors (73% of wrong rollouts, figure 9a). the two largest causes are misjudging a position, direction, or path in an image (31%) and miscounting objects (23%)
while reliability is equally critical in agentic workflows (section 5.3), we scope hfe to single-turn tasks so that results reflect the model rather than external tools or agent harnesses.
top models achieve 99.3% to 100% family pass@4, solving nearly every task family on at least one rollout.
hfe thus measures reliability on elementary tasks selected to expose model blind spots rather than a uniform sample of everyday queries
relying on one model family for grading could introduce subtle same-provider bias.

our human baseline evaluated seed prompts only (25% of the final benchmark, not the three sibling variants) using single-attempt, unassisted raters rather than repeated multi-variant trials (human family pass4 ).

we introduced humanitys first exam (hfe), a benchmark of 544 text and multimodal prompts (136 four-prompt task families) for measuring the foundational reliability of llms on elementary tasks that humans can easily solve.
today, were launching the humanitys first exam (hfe) benchmark on kaggle to measure how reliably llms answer straightforward, everyday questions.
instead of focusing on whether a model is capable of solving a task once, hfe measures whether models can consistently solve tasks (and slight variations) every single time.
the dataset consists of 544 elementary text and image prompts across 20 foundational capabilities.
over the last 6 months, frontier models have made significant progress on hfe.
through december 15 and submit everyday questions that todays models still get wrong.

example prompt from humanitys first exams public dataset: list the color of the third letter of each word in the neon sign in order, separated by a semicolon. (answer: green; yellow; white; blue; blue)
were launching humanitys first exam and a kaggle hackathon to test llm reliability.
oran kelly research scientist, google deepmind nov 24, 2026
